comparisons.title: CRP vs ESR
comparisons.intro: Both are 'inflammatory markers', and they are often ordered together, but they measure different things at different speeds. CRP is a single protein that rises and falls within days; the ESR is a physical property of blood that changes over weeks and is pushed up by many things besides inflammation.
comparisons.whenA: Tracking an acute infection or the response to antibiotics or surgery, where speed matters
comparisons.whenB: Suspected giant cell arteritis or polymyalgia, myeloma, and long-term monitoring of some rheumatic diseases

rows.a: Concentration of C-reactive protein, an acute-phase protein made by the liver
rows.b: How far red cells settle in a tube in one hour, a proxy for fibrinogen and immunoglobulins

rows.a: Rises within 6 hours, peaks at about 48 hours, falls quickly (half-life about 19 hours)
rows.b: Rises over days and falls over weeks

rows.a: Obesity, smoking and pregnancy raise it modestly
rows.b: Anaemia, pregnancy, age, kidney disease and high immunoglobulins raise it; polycythaemia and sickle cells lower it

rows.a: Infection and sepsis, post-operative monitoring, inflammatory bowel disease, point-of-care antibiotic decisions
rows.b: Giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis monitoring

rows.a: mg/L; laboratory upper limit, no diagnostic threshold
rows.b: mm/h; reference limit rises with age and differs by sex

rows.a: High CRP with normal ESR: early or minor inflammation
rows.b: High ESR with normal CRP: anaemia, pregnancy, lupus, myeloma or age

comparisons.title: Creatinine vs eGFR
comparisons.intro: Creatinine is the thing that is measured; eGFR is the number the laboratory calculates from it. They appear side by side on every kidney blood test, and confusing them is the commonest reason kidney results are misread.
comparisons.whenA: Detecting a change over hours to days (acute kidney injury), where the trend in the measured value matters and the estimate is invalid
comparisons.whenB: Staging chronic kidney disease, adjusting drug doses and comparing people of different ages and sexes

rows.a: A muscle waste product measured directly in blood
rows.b: An estimate of filtration calculated from creatinine, age and sex (CKD-EPI equation)

rows.a: Rises as kidney function falls
rows.b: Falls as kidney function falls

rows.a: µmol/L (UK) or mg/dL (US)
rows.b: mL/min/1.73 m²

rows.a: Higher in muscular people, lower in frail people, for the same kidney function
rows.b: Partly corrected by age and sex, but still misleading at extremes of muscle mass

rows.a: Valid at any time, but lags behind an acute change in filtration
rows.b: Only valid when kidney function is stable; not used in acute kidney injury

rows.a: Reference interval set by the laboratory
rows.b: Chronic kidney disease staging thresholds (below 60 for 3 months = CKD stage G3 or worse)

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management

comparisons.title: ECG vs echocardiogram
comparisons.intro: One records the heart's electricity, the other shows its structure and motion. They answer different questions and are usually both needed when heart disease is suspected.
comparisons.whenA: Chest pain, palpitations, blackouts, suspected heart attack or rhythm problem; a first test in minutes
comparisons.whenB: Breathlessness with a raised BNP, murmurs and valve disease, after a heart attack, heart failure staging

rows.a: Electrical rhythm, rate, conduction and signs of ischaemia, injury or strain over 10 seconds
rows.b: Chamber sizes, wall thickness and motion, pumping function (ejection fraction), valves and pressures in real time

rows.a: Ten electrodes on the chest and limbs; painless, no radiation, under 5 minutes
rows.b: Ultrasound probe with gel on the chest for 20-40 minutes; no radiation; a transoesophageal version for detailed views

rows.a: Arrhythmias, acute coronary syndromes (ST elevation), conduction block, electrolyte effects, QT prolongation
rows.b: Heart failure, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, pericardial fluid, sources of embolism, congenital disease

rows.a: Pumping function, valve disease or coronary anatomy; may be normal early in a heart attack
rows.b: The rhythm over time or the coronary arteries themselves

rows.a: Automated interpretation confirmed by a clinician, often at the bedside
rows.b: A sonographer or cardiologist, with a structured report

rows.a: First-line, repeated serially with troponin
rows.b: Ordered when the ECG, symptoms or BNP raise a structural question

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

comparisons.title: CT vs MRI
comparisons.intro: Both produce cross-sectional images of the body, but by different physics: CT uses X-rays and is fast, MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves and shows soft tissue in more detail without radiation. The choice depends on the question, the urgency and the patient.
comparisons.whenA: Emergencies (trauma, stroke within minutes, bleeding, pulmonary embolism), bone and lung detail, people who cannot lie still or have MRI-incompatible implants
comparisons.whenB: Brain and spinal cord, joints, ligaments and cartilage, the pelvis, liver lesions, and when radiation must be avoided

rows.a: Rotating X-ray beam and detectors reconstruct slices from tissue density
rows.b: Strong magnetic field and radio pulses map hydrogen nuclei; sequences highlight different tissue properties

rows.a: Yes: a moderate dose that adds up with repeated scans
rows.b: None

rows.a: Seconds to a few minutes
rows.b: 20-60 minutes, lying still in a narrow tunnel

rows.a: Bone, lung, acute bleeding, calcification, contrast-enhanced vessels
rows.b: Brain, spinal cord, muscle, ligaments, cartilage, pelvic organs, marrow

rows.a: Iodinated contrast (allergy and kidney precautions; metformin paused)
rows.b: Gadolinium (avoided in severe kidney impairment)

rows.a: Radiation, less soft-tissue detail, iodine contrast risks
rows.b: Metal implants and devices, claustrophobia, cost and availability, motion

comparisons.title: TSH vs free T4
comparisons.intro: TSH comes from the pituitary and free T4 from the thyroid, and they move in opposite directions. Reading them together tells whether a thyroid problem is mild or severe and whether it starts in the gland or in the pituitary.
comparisons.whenA: Screening for thyroid disease and adjusting levothyroxine, because it is the most sensitive single measure
comparisons.whenB: Judging severity, following treatment in the first weeks, and in pituitary disease where TSH cannot be trusted

rows.b: Thyroid gland (as thyroxine, T4)

rows.b: Rises

rows.b: Changes more slowly and stays within range in mild (subclinical) disease

rows.a: Takes about 6 weeks to settle
rows.b: Changes within days

rows.a: Pituitary disease, the first trimester, severe illness, biotin supplements
rows.b: Binding-protein changes are avoided by measuring the free fraction; heparin and biotin can interfere

comparisons.title: HbA1c vs blood glucose
comparisons.intro: Blood glucose is a snapshot of one moment; HbA1c is a three-month average. Both diagnose diabetes, but they answer different questions and each fails in different circumstances.
comparisons.whenA: Diagnosing and monitoring type 2 diabetes without fasting, and setting treatment targets
comparisons.whenB: Suspected type 1 diabetes, hypoglycaemia, pregnancy, acute illness, and any situation where red-cell lifespan is abnormal

rows.a: The fraction of haemoglobin with glucose attached, reflecting average glucose over 2-3 months
rows.b: Glucose concentration in blood at the time of sampling

rows.a: None; no fasting
rows.b: Fasting for 8-12 hours for a fasting test; timed after a glucose drink for a tolerance test

rows.a: 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above, repeated unless symptomatic
rows.b: Fasting 7.0 mmol/L or above, or 11.1 mmol/L two hours after a 75 g glucose load

rows.a: Very little
rows.b: Large: meals, exercise, stress and illness move it within hours

rows.a: Anaemia, haemolysis, transfusion, pregnancy, haemoglobin variants, kidney failure, suspected type 1 diabetes
rows.b: Delayed samples without fluoride, meter inaccuracy, acute stress

rows.a: Every 3-6 months for treatment targets
rows.b: Daily self-monitoring on insulin; continuous glucose monitoring

comparisons.title: Atorvastatin vs rosuvastatin
comparisons.intro: The two high-intensity statins share a mechanism and most of their effects. They differ in potency per milligram, in how they are cleared, and therefore in which other medicines and conditions limit their dose. This comparison describes those differences; the choice of statin and dose is made by a prescriber.
comparisons.whenA: The usual first choice in UK guidance (20 mg for primary prevention, 80 mg for secondary prevention); no dose limit in kidney impairment
comparisons.whenB: An alternative when atorvastatin is not tolerated or targets are not met, or when CYP3A4 interactions are a problem; dose capped by kidney function and ethnicity

rows.b: Statin; HMG-CoA reductase

rows.b: About 45-63% across 5-40 mg (roughly twice as potent per milligram)

rows.b: Minimal CYP metabolism; levels raised by ciclosporin (contraindicated), gemfibrozil, some HIV medicines; grapefruit irrelevant
